I own neither a pick-up, crossover, nor a full-size van (I own an SUV for recreational offroading), but let me try to answer...

In short:

Crossover Full-Size Van Pick-Up
Factory Off-Road Capability OK Poor Good
Ride Quality Good Poor OK
Dirty Cargo Poor Poor/OK Good
Cargo Access Restricted Restricted Public
Cargo Capacity Poor/OK Good Best
Towing Capacity Poor/OK Good Best
Marketing Vibe Soccer Mom Businesses Tough, Manly
Holds Fat People Poor Poor/OK Good

Off-Road Capability

You can get a variety of wheelbase lengths in pickups. Shorter wheelbases are better for getting over steep/tall, short obstacles. Longer wheelbases are better for getting started up long, steep hills. I have seen far less available variation in the wheelbase of crossovers and vans. This makes it easier to choose a pick-up with the correct wheelbase for your situation.

Many pick ups come from the factory with significantly higher ground clearance than vans and crossovers - both minimum clearance, which matters for getting over obstacles, and body lift, which matters if you're ever going to go through water or mud... Or want to put larger tires on to increase your minimum ground clearance (trying to put larger tires on almost any stock van or crossover wouuld result in them scraping the body: you would have to spend time and or money to lift the body, before you could put larger tires on).

I'll be honest: I don't really know what four-wheel-drive options are usually available on full-size vans. Most crossovers in the US will have some form of all-wheel drive or electronic help-you-skid-less two-wheel-drive. However, I do know that just about every conceivable four-wheel-drive drivetrain and style can be found on some pickup in the US. People who need an off-road utility vehicle know this too. A prime example would be a locking differential, something needed for aggressive off-road use. Good luck finding a crossover that comes with one! (again, I don't know about the vans)

Ride Quality

As the most car-like, crossovers win this category. However, among comparable cargo capacities...

The body of pick ups is usually shorter and wider than the body of a van, and the cross-section (which will catch wind and raise the center of gravity, making it more likely to tip over or at least causing you to experience more body roll when turning ) Is almost always less, especially if the pickup does not have a camper shell on the back. This likely leads to a smoother, more enjoyable drive without really giving up any capability.

Dirty Cargo

As mentioned elsewhere, you can absolutely hose down the bed of the pickup - or just do nothing as you take the car through a regular, automatic car wash - to clean the results of dirty cargo. Van/crossover, not so much.

If you are transporting any cargo with an odor or fumes, it can be hugely advantageous or downright necessary to have an open area in the back, separated from the cabin. You will never see a landscaping crew transporting the gas cans for their equipment in the enclosed cabin of a cargo van... At least not for very long.

Cargo Access

The open bed pick ups are better suited towards hauling things without storing them, and for multi person/shared access to those things, as you might experience taking furniture home from a store, helping somebody move, or carrying the stuff you are using when you and your group are going camping. An enclosed van with lockable doors implies more restricted access... that's why I usually see, at least around here, businesses with high-value density parts like telecom and plumbing use the vans while businesses with lower value density parts like landscaping use pick ups.

Cargo Capacity

You may be able to fit a lot of stuff in a crossover - maybe even enough for most people. You will unarguably be able to fit more in a van.

An open-bed pickup is unquestionably king of cargo capacity, as you are not limited to the vehicles' "cargo space," but just to what you can secure and the clearance of the road. Additionally, if the thing is particularly large or heavy, a crane can lift it out of and load it into the bed of the pickup. Not so much a crossover or van.

There are some cargo-carrying use cases that can never be fulfilled by a crossover or van.

Towing Capability

Not everyone needs to tow a full-size tractor-trailer trailer with their daily driver, but if they do (or something close to that), they'll use a goose-neck trailer on the back of a dually diesel pickup - crossovers and vans just cannot put out the traction, torque, and frame strength to tow the heaviest of the heavy things. The bed of a pickup can be converted to function like the hitch of an 18-wheeler semi and accept the heaviest trailers - vans and crossovers cannot do this.

Most crossovers are likely "unibody" construction, whereas it's much more likely to find a pickup with a "body-on-frame" construction. Body-on-frame is generally better for vehicles that will be under repeated, significant stresses (as might come from hauling cargo and towing).

Style

And let's be honest, there are people working on making pick up trucks look cool (at least to their target market, here in the US), and no one is really doing that with the vans, which are just pure utility vehicles. Crossovers (at least in the US) still have a "soccer-mom" or effeminate vibe... and at least around here in Texas, I see just as many petite women driving monstrous pickups as I do men. Anecdotally, they say they feel "safer" in the large, imposing, "tough" vehicles.

Fat People

Continuing to be honest, a lot of Americans are very, very large. Just like there's an upper limit to towing capability that crossovers and vans just can't cross and must be handled by a pickup, so too is there a body size above which you just won't fit in anything else. As more and more Americans cross that threshold, more and more pickups hit the roads...

Reasons to Pass in Europe

Don' Need No Car

Europe is generally much better about having walkable & public-transit cities where cars aren't necessary. A walkable city where cars aren't necessary usually means that a.) you can purchase everything you need from a store withing walkable/public transit distance of where you live, b.) you can walk/public transit to work, and c.) things you can't personally carry can be ordered for delivery. If you don't need a car, you certainly don't need a pickup! If you do need a car, still 2 of the 3 possible reasons for needing one wouldn't be served by a pickup.

It's Smaller

Of the European cities I've been to, the streets are almost universally narrower, the lanes are narrower, the parking spaces narrower, the clearances lower, and the corners tighter than in the US. Smaller vehicles are at a huge advantage here, and that incentivizes people to choose to just pay for someone else to drive the truck/van and deliver/transport cargo rather than personally own and drive a vehicle that could do it - unless you are the delivery-driver, the hassle doesn't end up being worth it.

Lock it Up!

Europe has a far higher population density in most areas than the US. The law of large numbers means that it's more likely that a thief will see your car, and an open-bed pickup with valuables in it is much more risky than a lockable, opaque van.

Cost of Operation

In the US, fuel prices are significantly cheaper than in Europe. Additionally, America makes, sells, and buys more pickups in America than Europe makes, sells, and buys in Europe. These two things make it harder to offset the monetary cost of owning a pickup with the opportunity cost of not being able to truck your own stuff around whenever you want:

If you drive a pickup with a huge hauling capacity, you're paying for that every mile you drive whether you're actually hauling anything or not - in fuel, and in the periodic maintenance and repairs. If you need that capacity twice a month, it's for sure cheaper to have your own truck than to pay someone else for the use of their truck, 24 times a year. But if you only really need the pickup's capacity once a year, maybe it's cheaper to just pay someone that one time.

In Europe, with higher fuel prices, that extra cost paid every mile for the higher-capacity vehicle is higher, and encourages people to take a closer look at the cost/benefit ratio and maybe forgo the pickup. In America, the lower total cost of fuel means more people can "get away with" having that extra capacity "just in case" without actually having to crunch the numbers... so even in identical situations, you'll see Europeans passing on pickups more often.

Furthermore, just how European import car service and parts are usually more expensive than equivalent domestic cars in the US, so too are American cars and parts usually more expensive than an equivalent European vehicle. Since there aren't a ton of pickups being made and sold in Europe, people are more likely to buy an American one, and getting it serviced is therefore likely to be harder and more expensive - again, encouraging people to skip buying a pickup unless they really truly need it.
